title: Investigatio motuum, quibus laminae et virgae elasticae contremiscunt

deep.reconstruction:
Problem II (§9) asks for the 'regular' motions of a vibrating elastic rod, meaning motions in which every point moves like a simple pendulum of length k. On the previous page Euler requires (1/2g) y_tt = −y/k. Here g is Euler's usual constant, the distance fallen from rest in one second. Treating s as a parameter, this gives y = M(s) sin(ζ + t√(2g/k)). The rod's equation of motion is (1/2g) y_tt = −b c² y_ssss. Substituting gives the spatial ODE b c² k y'''' = y. Writing f⁴ = b c² k, this becomes f⁴ y'''' = y. The trial solution y = e^{λs} gives λ⁴ = 1/f⁴.

On this page Euler lists the four roots ±1/f and ±i/f. He forms the complete integral y = α e^{s/f} + β e^{−s/f} + γ e^{is/f} + δ e^{−is/f}, which has four arbitrary constants. He then replaces the imaginary pair by sin(s/f) and cos(s/f), silently redefining γ and δ.

With s held fixed the constants may depend on t, so he writes them with a common factor N(t). Matching this with M(s) sin(ζ + t√(2g/k)) gives N = C sin(ζ + t√(2g/k)) and M = C(α e^{s/f} + β e^{−s/f} + γ sin(s/f) + δ cos(s/f)). The result is the separated (normal-mode) solution y = C sin(ζ + t√(2g/k)) · (α e^{s/f} + β e^{−s/f} + γ sin(s/f) + δ cos(s/f)). In modern terms this is X(s) = A cosh(λs) + B sinh(λs) + C sin(λs) + D cos(λs) for the Euler–Bernoulli beam.

On the next page the vibration time is π√(k/2g) and the frequency is √(2g)/(π√k) vibrations per second, counting half-oscillations as vibrations. This is Euler's standard convention. The boundary conditions, which fix f and hence k through a transcendental equation, are applied later in the memoir.
errors: Euler reuses γ and δ for the real sin/cos coefficients after converting the complex exponentials. This is a harmless relabelling of constants.

The step 'multiplying by a common factor N' is phrased loosely. Logically, the constants of the s-integration may be arbitrary functions of t, and the separable form follows from matching with M(s)·sin(...). Euler only exhibits sufficiency ('facillime praestabitur'), not that this is the only way to match.

ideas.what: Separation of variables / normal-mode (standing-wave) ansatz for the transverse vibration equation of an elastic rod
ideas.modern_name: Normal modes of the Euler–Bernoulli beam equation via separation of variables
ideas.usually_credited_to: Daniel Bernoulli and Euler (1734–1744), with Euler's 1744 Additamentum on elastic curves
ideas.where_published: Euler, Methodus inveniendi (1744), Additamentum I (E65); Euler's 1730s–1740s correspondence with D. Bernoulli; E526 revisits this in 1779/1782

ideas.what: Solving the constant-coefficient linear ODE f⁴y'''' = y by an exponential trial function, with complex roots converted to sin and cos
ideas.modern_name: Characteristic equation method for linear ODEs with constant coefficients
ideas.where_published: E62, De integratione aequationum differentialium altiorum graduum (Misc. Berol. 1743)

ideas.what: Frequency (pitch) of a rod mode obtained from the equivalent simple-pendulum length k = f⁴/(b c²), with the vibration count taken as the measure of the tone
ideas.modern_name: Dispersion relation ω ∝ λ² for beam modes

deep.surprise_reason: This is a textbook-standard derivation: the separation ansatz and the exp/sinh/sin/cos general solution of y'''' = y/f⁴. Euler had already published it decades earlier, and it is well covered in Truesdell's history of rational elastic mechanics. Nothing new appears on this page.
transcription_corrections: No substantive errors. The image writes the second exponent as e^{(−s)/f}, with the minus sign over the s; this is equivalent to e^{−s/f}.
In the final formula the printed text is 'y = C (ſin.(ζ + t√(2g/k))) (α e^{s/f} + β e^{−s/f} + γ ſin. s/f + δ coſ. s/f)', matching the transcription.
